title: Little words, and farewell
goal: Close the module with something no grammar book covers: the little words that make your sentences sound spoken by a person, not read off a page.
bekal: use *jæja*, *sko*, *nú*, *jú*, and *bara* in the right places
end a conversation with natural phrases
look back over all twenty units on one page

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Síðasti tíminn
dialogs.intro: The last class. Anna, Sigga, and Búdí sit in the same room as in unit 1 — but the conversation is completely different now.

notes: **Little words don't add meaning — they add tone.** *Jæja*, *nú*, *sko*, *bara*, *jú*, *ha*. A sentence without them is still correct, but sounds read from a book. With them, it sounds spoken by a person.

**Jæja is the most Icelandic word there is.** It can mean "well", "so", "all right", "let's get going", or "oh well", depending on tone and length. Said while getting up from a chair, it means "I'm off". If you could take only one word from this unit, take this one.
**Jú, not já.** Búdí answers *jú* because Anna's question seems to deny something he can do. The rule from unit 2 comes back in the last lines of this module — and now you use it without thinking.

**Sko is used for emphasis, like a stressed "really" in English.** *Þú ert **sko** orðinn Íslendingur* — you've **really** become an Icelander. It goes after the verb, and never at the start of a sentence.
**Complaining about the weather is a sign of citizenship.** Sigga's joke isn't empty: for Icelanders, complaining about the wind is the friendliest small talk there is — the national icebreaker.

**Þetta reddast is the unofficial motto of the Icelandic nation.** It means "this will work itself out". It's said about the weather, money, work, and volcanoes. It's the attitude of a people who have lived for a thousand years in an unpredictable place — and the most fitting last line for this module.

grammars.title: Little words that change the tone
body: None of them translates exactly. Learn them from examples, not from meanings.
after: You don't learn these by memorizing but by **noticing**. Listen to where Icelanders slip in *nú* and *sko*, then copy where they put them. Within a few weeks they'll come out on their own.
⚠️ Don't use too many at once. One little word per sentence is enough; two or three make you sound like you're imitating, not speaking.

after: Four cases, three genders, three tenses, and sentences without a doer — that's the complete framework of Icelandic. What you don't have yet isn't new rules but hours of practice.
The most honest measure of your progress is on page 1: read the unit 1 dialogue now, without looking at the translation. What once felt impossible now reads almost like English.

sections.title: Expressions that didn't fit any unit

blocks.text: These sentences are used too often to skip, but don't fit any grammar chapter. Learn them whole.

blocks.title: The two most often misunderstood
items: *Takk fyrir mig* is literally "thanks for me", and it's said **by the guest to the host** after a meal or visit. If you're the host, the reply is *takk fyrir komuna* — thanks for coming.
*Hvað segirðu gott?* is literally "what good do you say?" and just means "how are you?". The answer is *allt gott* or *bara fínt* — not a long story.
